Let $Q$ be the amount of agent in the basin at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which agent enters the tank minus the rate at which agent leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which agent enters the basin.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.05\,\text{kg/L}$ of the agent enters the basin at a rate of $8\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *agent* enters the basin is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (8\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (8\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0.4\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which agent exits the basin.

To find the rate at which agent leaves the basin, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the basin at time $t.$

The basin initially contains $320\,\text{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at $8\,\text{L/min}$ and leaves at $4\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the volume of liquid in the basin after $t$ minutes is 

$$
320+8t-4t=(320+4t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of agent in the basin, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{320+4t}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $4\,\text{L/min},$ *agent* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(4\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{320+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(4\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{320+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{4Q}{320+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{Q}{80+t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.4-\frac{Q}{80+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{80+t}Q=0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 1/(80+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|80+t|} \\  & =80+t\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=80+t$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(80+t)\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{1}{80+t}Q) & =(80+t)\cdot 0.4 \\ (80+t)\frac{dQ}{dt}+Q & =0.4(80+t) \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(80+t)) & =0.4(80+t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(80+t))\,dt & =\int 0.4(80+t)\,dt \\ Q(80+t) & =0.4\cdot \frac{1}{2}(80+t)^{2}+C \\ Q(t) & =0.2(80+t)+\frac{C}{80+t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the basin initially contains $2.2\,\text{kg}$ of agent. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=2.2,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =2.2 \\ 0.2(80+0)+\frac{C}{80+0} & =2.2 \\ 16+\frac{C}{80} & =2.2 \\ \frac{C}{80} & =-13.8 \\ C & =-1104\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.2(80+t)-\frac{1104}{80+t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,  the amount of agent in the basin $5$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(5) & =0.2(80+5)-\frac{1104}{80+5} \\  & =17-\frac{1104}{85} \\  & ≈4.01\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.
